topic: Present Simple and Present Continuous; action and state verbs
rule_en: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts and permanent situations. Use the present continuous for actions happening now, temporary situations, and fixed future arrangements (with a time expression). Some verbs describing states (know, like, want, believe, own, seem) are not normally used in the continuous form, even when the meaning is 'now'.
structure: Present Simple: subject + base verb (+s); Present Continuous: subject + am/is/are + verb-ing
examples_en: I usually cook dinner, but tonight my brother is cooking.
She knows the answer already.
We're meeting the new manager at three o'clock.
He believes every word she says.
tip: Don't say 'I am knowing' or 'She is wanting' — state verbs like know, want, believe stay in the simple form.

options: I know him well.
I am knowing him well.
I known him well.
questions.answer: I know him well.
questions.explanation: Know is a state verb — no continuous form.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about now.
options: Look, it's raining!
Look, it rains!
Look, it rain!
questions.answer: Look, it's raining!
questions.explanation: An action happening right now needs the continuous.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a fixed future plan.
options: We're flying to Rome on Friday.
We fly to Rome on Friday, always.
We flying to Rome on Friday.
questions.answer: We're flying to Rome on Friday.
questions.explanation: Present continuous with a time expression shows a fixed arrangement.

options: This soup tastes amazing.
This soup is tasting amazing.
This soup taste amazing.
questions.answer: This soup tastes amazing.
questions.explanation: Taste (=have a flavour) is a state verb here.

options: She goes to the gym every morning.
She is going to the gym every morning.
She going to the gym every morning.
questions.answer: She goes to the gym every morning.
questions.explanation: A routine needs the present simple.

options: I think you're right.
I'm thinking you're right.
I thinking you're right.
questions.answer: I think you're right.
questions.explanation: Think (=have an opinion) is a state verb here.

topic: future forms: Present Continuous, be going to, will/won't
rule_en: Use 'be going to' for plans and intentions decided before speaking, and for predictions based on present evidence. Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements with other people, usually with a time expression. Use 'will' for instant decisions, promises, offers, and predictions based on opinion rather than evidence.
structure: be going to + infinitive; Present Continuous (fixed arrangements); will/won't + infinitive
examples_en: We're going to repaint the kitchen next month.
Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.
I'm meeting Farida for lunch tomorrow.
I think our team will win the final.
I'll carry that bag for you.
tip: 'Will' is for a decision made at the moment of speaking; 'be going to' is for a decision made earlier.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence for a plan made last week.
options: We're going to visit my parents this weekend.
We will visit my parents this weekend.
We visit my parents this weekend.
questions.answer: We're going to visit my parents this weekend.
questions.explanation: A plan decided earlier uses 'be going to'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence for an instant decision.
options: The phone's ringing — I'll answer it.
The phone's ringing — I'm going to answer it.
The phone's ringing — I answer it.
questions.answer: The phone's ringing — I'll answer it.
questions.explanation: 'Will' is for decisions made at the moment of speaking.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence for a prediction based on evidence.
options: Look at the sky — it's going to snow.
Look at the sky — it will snow.
Look at the sky — it snows.
questions.answer: Look at the sky — it's going to snow.
questions.explanation: Present evidence takes 'be going to'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence for a fixed arrangement.
options: I'm having dinner with Aziz on Saturday.
I have dinner with Aziz on Saturday.
I will having dinner with Aziz on Saturday.
questions.answer: I'm having dinner with Aziz on Saturday.
questions.explanation: An arrangement with another person at a fixed time takes the present continuous.

options: I'll help you with those bags.
I'm going to help you with those bags.
I help you with those bags.
questions.answer: I'll help you with those bags.
questions.explanation: Offers use 'will'.

questions.text: Choose the correct prediction based on opinion.
options: I think prices will rise next year.
I think prices are rising next year.
I think prices go to rise next year.
questions.answer: I think prices will rise next year.
questions.explanation: An opinion-based prediction uses 'will'.

topic: Present Perfect and Past Simple
rule_en: Use the present perfect for past actions with a connection to now (no finished time given), for life experiences, and for recent news. Use the past simple for finished actions at a definite time in the past, often with a time expression like 'yesterday' or 'in 2019'.
structure: Present Perfect: have/has + past participle; Past Simple: verb + -ed / irregular form
examples_en: I've already finished the report.
She visited Samarkand last summer.
Have you ever tried plov?
We moved to this city in 2018.
tip: Never use a finished time expression (yesterday, last week, in 2015) with the present perfect.

options: I saw that film yesterday.
I've seen that film yesterday.
I have see that film yesterday.
questions.answer: I saw that film yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' is a finished time — use the past simple.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about experience.
options: Have you ever been to Turkey?
Did you ever been to Turkey?
Have you ever went to Turkey?
questions.answer: Have you ever been to Turkey?
questions.explanation: Life experience with no specific time — present perfect.

options: She graduated in 2020.
She has graduated in 2020.
She has graduate in 2020.
questions.answer: She graduated in 2020.
questions.explanation: A specific finished year takes the past simple.

options: The president has just arrived.
The president arrived just now yesterday.
The president has arrived yesterday.
questions.answer: The president has just arrived.
questions.explanation: Recent news with a present-relevance uses the present perfect.

options: I haven't finished my homework yet.
I didn't finished my homework yet.
I haven't finish my homework yet.
questions.answer: I haven't finished my homework yet.
questions.explanation: 'Yet' with an unfinished situation needs the present perfect.

options: We met them at the conference last year.
We've met them at the conference last year.
We have meet them at the conference last year.
questions.answer: We met them at the conference last year.
questions.explanation: 'Last year' is a definite finished time.

topic: Present Perfect + for/since; Present Perfect Continuous
rule_en: Use 'for' with a period of time (for two years) and 'since' with a point in time (since 2019) to show how long a situation has continued. Use the present perfect continuous to emphasise the duration or repetition of an activity that started in the past and continues now, or has just stopped, often leaving visible results.
structure: have/has + been + verb-ing; ... + for + period / since + point in time
examples_en: She has worked here for six years.
They have lived in Dushanbe since 2015.
I've been waiting for an hour.
Why are you so tired? — I've been cleaning all morning.
tip: Use 'for' with a length of time, 'since' with a starting point.

options: I've known her for ten years.
I've known her since ten years.
I know her for ten years.
questions.answer: I've known her for ten years.
questions.explanation: 'For' introduces a period of time.

options: He's lived here since 2016.
He's lived here for 2016.
He lives here since 2016.
questions.answer: He's lived here since 2016.
questions.explanation: 'Since' introduces a starting point.

options: I've been studying for three hours.
I've studied for three hours ago.
I study since three hours.
questions.answer: I've been studying for three hours.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasises ongoing duration.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence explaining a visible result.
options: Your hands are dirty — have you been gardening?
Your hands are dirty — have you gardened?
Your hands are dirty — you garden?
questions.answer: Your hands are dirty — have you been gardening?
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous explains a present result of a recent activity.

options: They've been married since 2010.
They've been married for 2010.
They married since 2010.
questions.answer: They've been married since 2010.
questions.explanation: 'Since' + a specific year.

options: We've been waiting here for ages.
We've waited here since ages.
We wait here for ages.
questions.answer: We've been waiting here for ages.
questions.explanation: Ongoing duration up to now — present perfect continuous.

topic: choosing between the comparative and superlative
rule_en: Use the comparative (-er / more + adjective + than) to compare two things. Use the superlative (the -est / the most + adjective) to compare one thing with all others in a group of three or more. Short adjectives usually add -er/-est; longer adjectives use more/most.
structure: comparative: adjective+er / more + adjective + than; superlative: the + adjective+est / the most + adjective
examples_en: This bus is faster than the old one.
Of all the buses, this one is the fastest.
The new phone is more expensive than mine.
It's the most expensive phone in the shop.
tip: Never combine both forms: not 'more faster', just 'faster'.

options: This road is narrower than that one.
This road is more narrower than that one.
This road is narrowest than that one.
questions.answer: This road is narrower than that one.
questions.explanation: Short adjective + -er, not 'more' + -er together.

options: He's the tallest player on the team.
He's the tallerest player on the team.
He's tallest player on the team.
questions.answer: He's the tallest player on the team.
questions.explanation: Superlative needs 'the' + adjective+est.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with a long adjective.
options: This film is more interesting than the last one.
This film is interestinger than the last one.
This film is the interesting than the last one.
questions.answer: This film is more interesting than the last one.
questions.explanation: Long adjectives use 'more' + adjective.

questions.text: Choose the correct superlative with a long adjective.
options: It's the most beautiful city I've seen.
It's the beautifulest city I've seen.
It's the more beautiful city I've seen.
questions.answer: It's the most beautiful city I've seen.
questions.explanation: Long adjective superlative: 'the most' + adjective.

options: She's the best cook in the family.
She's the goodest cook in the family.
She's the most good cook in the family.
questions.answer: She's the best cook in the family.
questions.explanation: 'Good' has an irregular superlative: best.

options: Today is colder than yesterday.
Today is more cold than yesterday.
Today is coldest than yesterday.
questions.answer: Today is colder than yesterday.
questions.explanation: Short adjective + -er for comparing two things.

topic: articles: a/an, the, and zero article
rule_en: Use 'a/an' to introduce something for the first time or talk about one of a general class. Use 'the' for something already mentioned, unique, or specific to both speakers. Use no article with plural or uncountable nouns in a general sense, and with most proper nouns.
structure: a/an + singular noun (first mention); the + noun (specific/known); Ø + plural/uncountable noun (general)
examples_en: I saw a dog in the park. The dog was barking loudly.
She's afraid of dogs in general.
The sun rises in the east.
He studies music at university.
tip: Don't add 'the' before general plural or uncountable nouns: not 'the music', just 'music', when speaking generally.

options: I bought a book yesterday. The book was excellent.
I bought book yesterday. Book was excellent.
I bought the book yesterday. A book was excellent.
questions.answer: I bought a book yesterday. The book was excellent.
questions.explanation: First mention: a; second mention: the.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about something unique.
options: The moon looked bright last night.
A moon looked bright last night.
Moon looked bright last night.
questions.answer: The moon looked bright last night.
questions.explanation: 'The moon' is unique, so it takes 'the'.

options: Cats are independent animals.
The cats are independent animals.
A cats are independent animals.
questions.answer: Cats are independent animals.
questions.explanation: General statement about a whole class uses no article with a plural noun.

options: She's studying medicine in France.
She's studying the medicine in France.
She's studying a medicine in France.
questions.answer: She's studying medicine in France.
questions.explanation: Uncountable noun used generally takes no article.

options: Can you pass me a spoon, please?
Can you pass me spoon, please?
Can you pass me the spoon, please, first time?
questions.answer: Can you pass me a spoon, please?
questions.explanation: Any one of several — use 'a'.

options: The Nile is the longest river in Africa.
Nile is the longest river in Africa.
A Nile is the longest river in Africa.
questions.answer: The Nile is the longest river in Africa.
questions.explanation: Names of rivers take 'the'.

topic: obligation and prohibition: have to, must, should
rule_en: Use 'must' for strong personal obligation and 'have to' for obligation coming from a rule or another person. Use 'mustn't' for prohibition (it is forbidden). Use 'should' for advice or a weaker recommendation, not an obligation.
structure: must/have to + infinitive; mustn't + infinitive (prohibition); should/shouldn't + infinitive (advice)
examples_en: I must call my mother tonight, I promised.
Employees have to wear a uniform here.
You mustn't smoke in this building.
You should drink more water every day.
tip: 'Don't have to' means it's not necessary; 'mustn't' means it's forbidden — they are very different.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a rule.
options: Students have to wear ID cards on campus.
Students must to wear ID cards on campus.
Students should wear ID cards on campus, it's the law.
questions.answer: Students have to wear ID cards on campus.
questions.explanation: An external rule is expressed with 'have to'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about prohibition.
options: You mustn't park here.
You don't have to park here.
You shouldn't to park here.
questions.answer: You mustn't park here.
questions.explanation: Prohibition is expressed with 'mustn't'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence meaning 'it's not necessary'.
options: You don't have to bring anything, we have everything.
You mustn't bring anything, we have everything.
You shouldn't to bring anything, we have everything.
questions.answer: You don't have to bring anything, we have everything.
questions.explanation: 'Don't have to' means something isn't necessary.

options: You should see a doctor about that cough.
You must to see a doctor about that cough.
You have see a doctor about that cough.
questions.answer: You should see a doctor about that cough.
questions.explanation: Advice, not obligation, uses 'should'.

questions.text: Choose the correct strong personal obligation.
options: I must finish this before Friday, it matters to me.
I must to finish this before Friday.
I having to finish this before Friday.
questions.answer: I must finish this before Friday, it matters to me.
questions.explanation: 'Must' + bare infinitive expresses personal obligation.

options: Passengers mustn't use phones during take-off.
Passengers don't have to use phones during take-off.
Passengers shouldn't to use phones during take-off.
questions.answer: Passengers mustn't use phones during take-off.
questions.explanation: A safety rule forbidding something needs 'mustn't'.

topic: ability and possibility: can, could, be able to
rule_en: Use 'can' for present ability and general possibility. Use 'could' for general past ability. Use 'was/were able to' for a specific past achievement (one occasion). 'Be able to' can replace 'can/could' in tenses where they don't exist, such as the future or present perfect.
structure: can/could + infinitive; be able to + infinitive (all tenses)
examples_en: She can speak four languages.
When I was young, I could run very fast.
Despite the storm, they were able to land safely.
I haven't been able to sleep well this week.
tip: For one specific past success, use 'was/were able to', not 'could'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about present ability.
options: He can fix almost anything.
He is able fix almost anything.
He could fix almost anything, now.
questions.answer: He can fix almost anything.
questions.explanation: General present ability uses 'can'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about general past ability.
options: As a child, I could climb trees easily.
As a child, I was able climb trees easily.
As a child, I can climb trees easily.
questions.answer: As a child, I could climb trees easily.
questions.explanation: General ability in the past uses 'could'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about one specific past success.
options: Despite the traffic, we were able to arrive on time.
Despite the traffic, we could arrive on time.
Despite the traffic, we can arrive on time.
questions.answer: Despite the traffic, we were able to arrive on time.
questions.explanation: A specific one-time achievement needs 'was/were able to'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with the future.
options: I'll be able to help you tomorrow.
I'll can help you tomorrow.
I'll could help you tomorrow.
questions.answer: I'll be able to help you tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Can' has no future form — use 'be able to'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence in the present perfect.
options: She hasn't been able to contact him.
She hasn't could contact him.
She hasn't can contact him.
questions.answer: She hasn't been able to contact him.
questions.explanation: 'Can' has no present perfect form — use 'be able to'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about possibility.
options: It can get very cold here in winter.
It could get very cold here in winter, generally.
It is able to get very cold here in winter, generally.
questions.answer: It can get very cold here in winter.
questions.explanation: General possibility uses 'can'.

topic: past tenses: simple, continuous and perfect
rule_en: Use the past simple for completed actions in sequence. Use the past continuous for a background action in progress, often interrupted by a past simple action. Use the past perfect for an action that happened before another past action or time, to show the order of events clearly.
structure: Past Simple: verb+ed; Past Continuous: was/were + verb-ing; Past Perfect: had + past participle
examples_en: While I was cooking, the phone rang.
By the time she arrived, the meeting had already started.
He opened the door and walked in.
They had finished dinner before the film began.
tip: Use the past perfect only when you need to show one past event happened clearly before another.

options: I was reading when the lights went out.
I read when the lights were going out.
I had read when the lights went out.
questions.answer: I was reading when the lights went out.
questions.explanation: Background action in progress, interrupted by a simple past event.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence showing order of events.
options: By six o'clock, everyone had left the office.
By six o'clock, everyone left the office.
By six o'clock, everyone was leaving the office.
questions.answer: By six o'clock, everyone had left the office.
questions.explanation: Past perfect shows the action finished before the stated past time.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence for a sequence of completed actions.
options: She stood up, took her bag, and left.
She was standing up, was taking her bag, and was leaving.
She had stood up, had taken her bag, and had left.
questions.answer: She stood up, took her bag, and left.
questions.explanation: A simple sequence of completed actions uses the past simple.

options: He was cooking dinner when I got home.
He cooked dinner when I was getting home.
He had cooked dinner when I was getting home, at that moment.
questions.answer: He was cooking dinner when I got home.
questions.explanation: Ongoing action interrupted by a simple past event.

options: The train had already left when we reached the station.
The train already left when we reached the station.
The train was already leaving when we reached the station.
questions.answer: The train had already left when we reached the station.
questions.explanation: The leaving happened before the arriving — past perfect.

options: We were having dinner when the guests arrived.
We had dinner when the guests were arriving.
We had had dinner when the guests arrived, at that exact moment.
questions.answer: We were having dinner when the guests arrived.
questions.explanation: Ongoing background action interrupted by an event.

topic: past and present habits: used to, usually
rule_en: Use 'used to' + infinitive for repeated past actions or states that are no longer true. Use the present simple with an adverb of frequency (usually, often, always) for current habits. 'Used to' only exists in the past — for present habits, use the present simple.
structure: used to + infinitive (past habit); present simple + adverb of frequency (current habit)
examples_en: I used to walk to school, but now I take the bus.
She usually gets up at six.
We didn't use to like spicy food.
He always checks his email before breakfast.
tip: 'Used to' has no present form: don't say 'I use to go' for a present habit — just use the present simple.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a past habit that has stopped.
options: I used to play the piano every day.
I use to play the piano every day.
I was used to play the piano every day.
questions.answer: I used to play the piano every day.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + infinitive for a discontinued past habit.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a current habit.
options: She usually eats breakfast at seven.
She used to eat breakfast at seven, now.
She use to eat breakfast at seven.
questions.answer: She usually eats breakfast at seven.
questions.explanation: Present habits use the present simple, not 'used to'.

options: We didn't use to have a car.
We didn't used to have a car.
We not used to have a car.
questions.answer: We didn't use to have a car.
questions.explanation: After 'didn't', use the base form 'use to', not 'used to'.

options: Did you use to live in the countryside?
Did you used to live in the countryside?
Do you used to live in the countryside?
questions.answer: Did you use to live in the countryside?
questions.explanation: Question form: did + subject + use to + infinitive.

options: He always arrives early to work.
He used to arrive early to work, currently.
He use to arriving early to work.
questions.answer: He always arrives early to work.
questions.explanation: A current habit takes the present simple with an adverb of frequency.

options: They used to live next door to us.
They use to living next door to us.
They are used to live next door to us.
questions.answer: They used to live next door to us.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + infinitive describes a past state that has changed.

topic: the passive (all tenses)
rule_en: Use the passive when the action is more important than who does it, or when the agent is unknown or obvious. Form the passive with the correct tense of 'be' + past participle. Add 'by + agent' only when it's important to say who did the action.
structure: subject + be (in correct tense) + past participle (+ by + agent)
examples_en: This bridge was built in 1932.
English is spoken in many countries.
The report will be finished by Friday.
The window has been broken.
tip: Only mention 'by + agent' if it adds useful information — often it's better left out.

options: The letters were sent yesterday.
The letters sent yesterday.
The letters were send yesterday.
questions.answer: The letters were sent yesterday.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct passive sentence about a general fact.
options: Rice is grown in many Asian countries.
Rice grows in many Asian countries by farmers.
Rice is growing in many Asian countries.
questions.answer: Rice is grown in many Asian countries.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive for a general fact.

questions.text: Choose the correct future passive sentence.
options: The results will be announced tomorrow.
The results will announce tomorrow.
The results are announced tomorrow, next.
questions.answer: The results will be announced tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Future passive: will + be + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct present perfect passive sentence.
options: The car has been repaired.
The car has repaired.
The car has been repair.
questions.answer: The car has been repaired.
questions.explanation: Present perfect passive: has/have been + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with an agent.
options: The novel was written by a young author.
The novel wrote by a young author.
The novel was written from a young author.
questions.answer: The novel was written by a young author.
questions.explanation: Agent introduced with 'by'.

options: This song is loved by millions of people.
This song loves by millions of people.
This song is love by millions of people.
questions.answer: This song is loved by millions of people.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive with an agent.

topic: modal verbs of deduction: might, can't, must
rule_en: Use 'must' when you are almost certain something is true, based on evidence. Use 'can't' when you are almost certain something is not true. Use 'might/could/may' when something is possible but you're not sure.
structure: must / can't / might + infinitive (present deduction); must / can't / might + have + past participle (past deduction)
examples_en: The lights are off — they must be asleep.
She can't be at work, it's Sunday.
He might know the answer — let's ask him.
They must have left already, the door is locked.
tip: 'Mustn't' is not used for deduction — for a negative certainty, use 'can't'.

options: He must be tired after that long journey.
He mustn't be tired after that long journey.
He can be tired after that long journey.
questions.answer: He must be tired after that long journey.
questions.explanation: Strong positive certainty uses 'must'.

options: That can't be true.
That mustn't be true.
That don't must be true.
questions.answer: That can't be true.
questions.explanation: Strong negative certainty uses 'can't', not 'mustn't'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence about a possibility.
options: She might be at the library.
She musts be at the library.
She can't be at the library, maybe.
questions.answer: She might be at the library.
questions.explanation: An uncertain possibility uses 'might'.

options: They must have forgotten the meeting.
They must forgot the meeting.
They must have forget the meeting.
questions.answer: They must have forgotten the meeting.
questions.explanation: Past deduction: must + have + past participle.

options: He can't have finished already, it's too soon.
He mustn't have finished already, it's too soon.
He might not have finish already, it's too soon.
questions.answer: He can't have finished already, it's too soon.
questions.explanation: Strong negative past deduction uses 'can't have'.

options: It might have rained last night, the ground is wet.
It mights have rained last night, the ground is wet.
It might have rain last night, the ground is wet.
questions.answer: It might have rained last night, the ground is wet.
questions.explanation: Uncertain past deduction: might + have + past participle.

topic: first conditional and future time clauses with when, until
rule_en: Use the first conditional (if + present, will + infinitive) for real future possibilities. Use future time clauses with when, until, as soon as, before, and after in the same way — the present tense in the time clause, 'will' in the main clause.
structure: If/When/Until + present simple, ... will + infinitive
examples_en: If it rains, we'll cancel the picnic.
When she arrives, we'll start the meeting.
I won't leave until you call me.
As soon as I finish, I'll send you the file.
tip: Never use 'will' after if, when, until or as soon as in these sentences — use the present simple instead.

options: If we hurry, we'll catch the bus.
If we will hurry, we'll catch the bus.
If we hurry, we catch the bus, definitely.
questions.answer: If we hurry, we'll catch the bus.
questions.explanation: Present simple after 'if', 'will' in the main clause.

options: When he calls, I'll tell him the news.
When he will call, I'll tell him the news.
When he calls, I tell him the news, always.
questions.answer: When he calls, I'll tell him the news.
questions.explanation: Present simple after 'when' for a future event.

options: I'll wait here until you finish.
I'll wait here until you'll finish.
I wait here until you finish, generally.
questions.answer: I'll wait here until you finish.
questions.explanation: Present simple after 'until', referring to the future.

options: As soon as the rain stops, we'll leave.
As soon as the rain will stop, we'll leave.
As soon as the rain stops, we leave, usually.
questions.answer: As soon as the rain stops, we'll leave.
questions.explanation: Present simple after 'as soon as' for the future.

options: If you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.
If you won't hurry, you'll miss the train.
If you don't hurry, you miss the train, always.
questions.answer: If you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.
questions.explanation: Negative present simple after 'if', 'will' in the main clause.

options: Before you leave, please turn off the lights.
Before you will leave, please turn off the lights.
Before you leaving, please turn off the lights.
questions.answer: Before you leave, please turn off the lights.
questions.explanation: Present simple after 'before' for a future time clause.

topic: second conditional; choosing between the first and second conditional
rule_en: Use the second conditional (if + past simple, would + infinitive) for unreal, hypothetical or unlikely present/future situations. Use the first conditional for realistic, likely situations. The choice between them shows how possible the speaker believes the situation is.
structure: If + past simple, ... would + infinitive
examples_en: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.
If I were you, I'd apologise.
If she studied harder, she would pass the exam.
If it rained tomorrow, we would stay home.
tip: In the second conditional, 'were' is often used for all subjects with the verb 'be': 'If I were...', not 'If I was...'.

options: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.
If I have more time, I would learn Spanish.
If I had more time, I will learn Spanish.
questions.answer: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: past simple + would + infinitive.

options: If I were rich, I'd buy a big house.
If I was rich, I'd buy a big house, formally.
If I be rich, I'd buy a big house.
questions.answer: If I were rich, I'd buy a big house.
questions.explanation: 'Were' is the standard form for all subjects in hypotheticals.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence for a realistic future plan.
options: If it rains tomorrow, we'll take umbrellas.
If it rained tomorrow, we would take umbrellas.
If it rains tomorrow, we would take umbrellas.
questions.answer: If it rains tomorrow, we'll take umbrellas.
questions.explanation: A realistic possibility uses the first conditional.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence for an unlikely situation.
options: If I met a celebrity, I would ask for a photo.
If I meet a celebrity, I would ask for a photo.
If I met a celebrity, I will ask for a photo.
questions.answer: If I met a celebrity, I would ask for a photo.
questions.explanation: An unlikely hypothetical situation uses the second conditional.

options: If she had a car, she wouldn't take the bus.
If she has a car, she wouldn't take the bus.
If she had a car, she won't take the bus.
questions.answer: If she had a car, she wouldn't take the bus.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: past simple + wouldn't + infinitive.

options: If you asked him nicely, he would help you.
If you ask him nicely, he would help you.
If you asked him nicely, he will help you.
questions.answer: If you asked him nicely, he would help you.
questions.explanation: Second conditional describes a hypothetical situation, not certain.

topic: choosing between the gerund and the infinitive
rule_en: Some verbs are followed by the gerund (verb+ing): enjoy, finish, avoid, suggest, mind. Some are followed by the infinitive with to: want, decide, hope, promise, agree. A few verbs (like, start, begin, love, hate) can take either with little difference in meaning.
structure: verb + gerund (verb-ing); verb + to-infinitive
examples_en: She suggested going to the new restaurant.
We decided to leave early.
I don't mind waiting a few minutes.
He promised to call back later.
tip: After a preposition, always use the gerund, never the infinitive: 'good at cooking', not 'good at to cook'.

options: They avoided answering the question.
They avoided to answer the question.
They avoided answer the question.
questions.answer: They avoided answering the question.
questions.explanation: 'Avoid' is followed by the gerund.

options: She agreed to help us move.
She agreed helping us move.
She agreed help us move.
questions.answer: She agreed to help us move.
questions.explanation: 'Agree' is followed by the to-infinitive.

options: He finished writing the report at noon.
He finished to write the report at noon.
He finished write the report at noon.
questions.answer: He finished writing the report at noon.
questions.explanation: 'Finish' is followed by the gerund.

options: We hope to visit you next year.
We hope visiting you next year.
We hope visit you next year.
questions.answer: We hope to visit you next year.
questions.explanation: 'Hope' is followed by the to-infinitive.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence after a preposition.
options: She's interested in learning French.
She's interested in to learn French.
She's interested learn French.
questions.answer: She's interested in learning French.
questions.explanation: After a preposition, use the gerund.

options: He suggested taking a different route.
He suggested to take a different route.
He suggested take a different route.
questions.answer: He suggested taking a different route.
questions.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by the gerund.

topic: reported speech: statements and questions
rule_en: When reporting statements, tenses usually move one step back into the past (present simple → past simple, present perfect → past perfect). When reporting questions, change the word order back to statement order and remove the auxiliary do/does/did; for yes/no questions, add 'if' or 'whether'.
structure: say/tell + (that) + clause (tense shifted back); ask + if/whether/question word + statement word order
examples_en: 'I'm tired,' she said. → She said she was tired.
'I'll call you,' he said. → He said he would call me.
'Do you like tea?' → She asked if I liked tea.
'Where do you live?' → He asked where I lived.
tip: In reported questions, the word order is the same as a statement — don't keep the question word order.

options: She said she was busy.
She said she is busy.
She said that she busy.
questions.answer: She said she was busy.
questions.explanation: Present simple shifts back to past simple in reported speech.

options: He said he would come later.
He said he will come later.
He said he comes later.
questions.answer: He said he would come later.
questions.explanation: 'Will' shifts back to 'would' in reported speech.

questions.text: Choose the correct reported yes/no question.
options: He asked if I was hungry.
He asked was I hungry.
He asked if I hungry.
questions.answer: He asked if I was hungry.
questions.explanation: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' + statement word order.

options: She asked where I worked.
She asked where did I work.
She asked where I work.
questions.answer: She asked where I worked.
questions.explanation: Statement word order, tense shifted back.

options: They said they had finished the project.
They said they have finished the project.
They said they finished the project, present.
questions.answer: They said they had finished the project.
questions.explanation: Present perfect shifts back to past perfect.

options: He asked what time it was.
He asked what time was it.
He asked what time it is.
questions.answer: He asked what time it was.
questions.explanation: Statement word order and past tense in reported questions.

topic: the third conditional
rule_en: Use the third conditional (if + past perfect, would have + past participle) to talk about hypothetical past situations that did not happen and their imagined results. It's often used to express regret or criticism about the past.
structure: If + past perfect, ... would have + past participle
examples_en: If I had known about the traffic, I would have left earlier.
She wouldn't have missed the train if she had woken up on time.
If they had studied harder, they would have passed.
I would have called you if I had had your number.
tip: Both parts of the sentence refer to an imaginary past — nothing here actually happened.

questions.text: Choose the correct third conditional sentence.
options: If I had seen you, I would have said hello.
If I saw you, I would have said hello.
If I had seen you, I would say hello.
questions.answer: If I had seen you, I would have said hello.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: past perfect + would have + past participle.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence expressing regret.
options: If I had studied medicine, I would have become a doctor.
If I studied medicine, I would have become a doctor.
If I had studied medicine, I become a doctor.
questions.answer: If I had studied medicine, I would have become a doctor.
questions.explanation: Third conditional describes an imagined past that didn't happen.

questions.text: Choose the correct negative third conditional.
options: She wouldn't have been late if she had left earlier.
She wouldn't be late if she had left earlier.
She wouldn't have been late if she left earlier.
questions.answer: She wouldn't have been late if she had left earlier.
questions.explanation: Both clauses need the third conditional forms.

options: If we had booked earlier, the tickets would have been cheaper.
If we booked earlier, the tickets would have been cheaper.
If we had booked earlier, the tickets would be cheaper, now.
questions.answer: If we had booked earlier, the tickets would have been cheaper.
questions.explanation: Both clauses refer to an unreal past.

options: He would have passed if he hadn't panicked.
He would pass if he hadn't panicked.
He would have passed if he didn't panicked.
questions.answer: He would have passed if he hadn't panicked.
questions.explanation: Negative past perfect in the if-clause.

options: If I had known, I wouldn't have said anything.
If I knew, I wouldn't have said anything.
If I had known, I wouldn't say anything.
questions.answer: If I had known, I wouldn't have said anything.
questions.explanation: Third conditional expressing regret about the past.

topic: quantifiers
rule_en: Use 'much' and 'a little' with uncountable nouns, 'many' and 'a few' with countable plural nouns, and 'a lot of/lots of' or 'some/any' with both. Use 'few' and 'little' (without 'a') to emphasise a small, often insufficient amount.
structure: much/a little/little + uncountable noun; many/a few/few + countable plural noun; a lot of/some/any + either
examples_en: We don't have much time left.
There are a few apples in the bowl.
She has little patience for excuses.
I need some advice about this.
Few people know the real story.
tip: 'A few/a little' sound positive (some, enough); 'few/little' (without 'a') sound negative (almost none).

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with an uncountable noun.
options: We don't have much money left.
We don't have many money left.
We don't have a few money left.
questions.answer: We don't have much money left.
questions.explanation: 'Money' is uncountable, so use 'much'.

questions.text: Choose the correct sentence with a countable noun.
options: There are many books on the shelf.
There is much books on the shelf.
There are a little books on the shelf.
questions.answer: There are many books on the shelf.
questions.explanation: 'Books' is countable plural, so use 'many'.

questions.text: Choose the sentence with a positive meaning.
options: We have a few minutes before the train leaves, that's fine.
We have few minutes before the train leaves, that's fine.
We have much minutes before the train leaves.
questions.answer: We have a few minutes before the train leaves, that's fine.
questions.explanation: 'A few' has a positive, sufficient meaning.

questions.text: Choose the sentence with a negative meaning.
options: Few people showed up to the meeting.
A few people showed up to the meeting, disappointingly.
Many people showed up to the meeting, disappointingly.
questions.answer: Few people showed up to the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Few' (without 'a') suggests an insufficient number.

options: She gave me a little advice before the interview.
She gave me a few advice before the interview.
She gave me many advice before the interview.
questions.answer: She gave me a little advice before the interview.
questions.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable, so use 'a little'.

options: Is there any milk left in the fridge?
Is there some milk left in the fridge, asking generally?
Are there any milk left in the fridge?
questions.answer: Is there any milk left in the fridge?
questions.explanation: 'Any' is typical in questions with uncountable nouns.

topic: relative clauses: defining and non-defining
rule_en: Defining relative clauses give essential information to identify the noun, with no commas (who, which, that, whose). Non-defining relative clauses add extra, non-essential information, marked off by commas, and cannot use 'that'.
structure: defining: noun + who/which/that + clause (no commas); non-defining: noun + , who/which + clause, (with commas)
examples_en: The woman who called earlier left a message.
My brother, who lives in Paris, is visiting next week.
This is the book that everyone is talking about.
Samarkand, which is a very old city, has beautiful architecture.
tip: You can never use 'that' in a non-defining relative clause, and you can never omit the commas.

questions.text: Choose the correct defining relative clause.
options: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
The man, who lives next door, is a doctor, essential info.
The man that, who lives next door, is a doctor.
questions.answer: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
questions.explanation: Defining clauses identify the noun and have no commas.

questions.text: Choose the correct non-defining relative clause.
options: My father, who is retired now, still wakes up early.
My father who is retired now still wakes up early.
My father, that is retired now, still wakes up early.
questions.answer: My father, who is retired now, still wakes up early.
questions.explanation: Non-defining clauses need commas and cannot use 'that'.

options: This is the film that won the award.
This is the film, that won the award.
This is the film who won the award.
questions.answer: This is the film that won the award.
questions.explanation: Defining clause with 'that' for a thing, no commas.

options: Dushanbe, which is the capital, has grown a lot.
Dushanbe which is the capital has grown a lot.
Dushanbe, that is the capital, has grown a lot.
questions.answer: Dushanbe, which is the capital, has grown a lot.
questions.explanation: Non-defining clause about a unique place needs commas and 'which'.

options: The girl whose bag was stolen called the police.
The girl who's bag was stolen called the police.
The girl, whose bag was stolen, called the police, essential.
questions.answer: The girl whose bag was stolen called the police.
questions.explanation: Defining clause with 'whose' showing possession, no commas needed.

options: The book which I borrowed from you was excellent.
The book, which I borrowed from you, was excellent, essential.
The book whom I borrowed from you was excellent.
questions.answer: The book which I borrowed from you was excellent.
questions.explanation: Defining clause about a thing uses 'which' or 'that', no commas.

topic: question tags
rule_en: Question tags are short questions added to the end of a statement to check information or invite agreement. A positive statement takes a negative tag; a negative statement takes a positive tag. The tag repeats the auxiliary verb (or uses do/does/did) and the subject pronoun.
structure: positive statement, negative tag?; negative statement, positive tag?
examples_en: You're coming to the party, aren't you?
She doesn't like coffee, does she?
They've finished the project, haven't they?
He can swim, can't he?
tip: After 'I am', the tag is 'aren't I?', not 'amn't I?'.

options: It's a lovely day, isn't it?
It's a lovely day, is it?
It's a lovely day, isn't he?
questions.answer: It's a lovely day, isn't it?
questions.explanation: Positive statement takes a negative tag matching the subject.

options: You don't smoke, do you?
You don't smoke, don't you?
You don't smoke, aren't you?
questions.answer: You don't smoke, do you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement takes a positive tag.

options: They live nearby, don't they?
They live nearby, do they?
They live nearby, aren't they?
questions.answer: They live nearby, don't they?
questions.explanation: Present simple positive statement, negative tag with 'don't'.

options: She'll be there, won't she?
She'll be there, will she?
She'll be there, isn't she?
questions.answer: She'll be there, won't she?
questions.explanation: 'Will' statement takes a 'won't' tag.

options: I'm right, aren't I?
I'm right, amn't I?
I'm right, isn't I?
questions.answer: I'm right, aren't I?
questions.explanation: 'I am' always takes the tag 'aren't I?'.

options: You haven't seen my keys, have you?
You haven't seen my keys, haven't you?
You haven't seen my keys, do you?
questions.answer: You haven't seen my keys, have you?
questions.explanation: Negative present perfect statement takes a positive 'have' tag.
